content: Tobacco and alcohol use significantly reduce the effectiveness of treatment for laryngeal cancer. Patients with laryngeal cancer who continue to smoke or drink are less likely to achieve a cure and are at an increased risk of developing secondary malignancies. Current smokers have a 10to 20-fold higher risk of developing laryngeal cancer compared to non-smokers. However, this risk decreases after smoking cessation, though it never returns to the baseline level of those who have never smoked. Approximately 10 to 15 years after quitting smoking, the relative risk is reduced by about 60%. Alcohol consumption is associated with an increased risk of cancers of the mouth, throat, esophagus, larynx, liver, and breast. Individuals consuming five or more alcoholic drinks per day have at least a 2to 3-fold higher risk of developing these cancers compared to non-drinkers. The combined use of alcohol and tobacco further amplifies the risk of these cancers. The risk is particularly high among individuals who consume large amounts of alcohol while also using tobacco. Lower socioeconomic status, which is often associated with inadequate healthcare, smoking, drinking, poor dietary habits, and exposure to environmental and occupational carcinogens, has been linked to an increased risk of cancer, including laryngeal cancer. Workplace carcinogens such as asbestos, nickel compounds, wood dust, leather products, paint, diesel fumes, and glass wool are also recognized risk factors. Additionally, a potential association between chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease or laryngopharyngeal reflux disease and laryngeal cancer remains controversial. The role of human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly subtypes 16 and 18, in laryngeal cancer is also uncertain, despite strong evidence linking these subtypes to oropharyngeal cancer. The World Health Organization classifies premalignant laryngeal lesions into categories such as hyperplasia, keratosis, mild, moderate, or severe dysplasia, and carcinoma in situ. Early lesions may show hyperkeratosis or parakeratosis without cellular atypia or dysplasia. Squamous cell dysplasia is characterized by cellular atypia and a loss of normal maturation and stratification. Mild dysplasia involves abnormalities limited to the basal third of the epithelium, moderate dysplasia affects up to two-thirds, and severe dysplasia involves more than two-thirds. Carcinoma in situ is an intraepithelial neoplasm where the full thickness of the squamous epithelium exhibits carcinoma-like features without breaching the basement membrane. Biopsy remains the gold standard for diagnosing premalignant laryngeal lesions, as visual appearance and laryngoscopic techniques cannot reliably differentiate between benign and malignant lesions. Techniques such as contact endoscopy with methylene blue staining and autofluorescence endoscopy have been explored, but their limitations include false positives and negatives, particularly in cases involving scarring, hyperkeratotic lesions, or inflammation. Optical coherence tomography, which uses near-infrared light to examine epithelial and subepithelial architecture, shows promise as a diagnostic tool. Management of premalignant laryngeal lesions depends on the severity of dysplasia. For mild and moderate dysplasia, either intervention or close follow-up is recommended. Severe dysplasia and carcinoma in situ, which carry a high risk of progression to invasive carcinoma, require medical or surgical treatment. Surgical excision using microlaryngoscopic techniques is common, and close follow-up is necessary due to the risk of recurrence and malignant transformation. Radiation therapy is generally not recommended for premalignant lesions but may be considered in rare cases of high-grade dysplasia with poor access. For early glottic cancer (T1/T2), transoral laser microsurgery (TLM) is recommended due to its favorable oncologic and functional outcomes, including voice preservation, shorter treatment duration, and comparable survival rates to radiotherapy. TLM is associated with low morbidity, reduced need for tracheostomy or nasogastric feeding, and shorter hospital stays. It is also easily repeatable and offers retreatment options for local recurrence. However, for cases involving the anterior commissure, the choice of treatment remains controversial due to the increased risk of local recurrence. Open partial laryngectomy may be considered in such cases, though it carries higher surgical morbidity. For advanced glottic cancer (T3/T4), total laryngectomy is often the primary surgical modality. In select cases, open partial laryngectomy may be performed to preserve laryngeal function, though it is associated with increased postoperative morbidity. Supracricoid laryngectomy with cricohyoidoepiglottopexy (SCL-CHEP) is another option for select T3 cases, offering high functional outcomes and local control rates exceeding 90%. However, this procedure is contraindicated in cases of arytenoid fixation, extensive cartilage infiltration, or extralaryngeal spread. Transoral laser microsurgery may also be considered for select T3 cases, though it carries a higher risk of positive margins and often requires adjuvant radiotherapy. In conclusion, the management of laryngeal cancer and premalignant lesions requires a tailored approach based on the stage and location of the disease, as well as the patient’s overall health and functional needs. Advanced surgical techniques, such as TLM and SCL, offer promising outcomes for organ preservation and functional recovery, but careful patient selection and surgeon expertise are critical to achieving optimal results.
